item.title: Qualcomm seeks deeper AI cooperation with China, citing its strengths in tech commercialization
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 19:03:00
The Qualcomm booth at the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) in Beijing on September 9, 2026. Photo: VCG US chipmaker Qualcomm is seeking to deepen cooperation with Chinese partners to bring artificial intelligence (AI) into more devices and industries, underscoring China's growing role in turning technological innovations into large-scale industrial applications, as US technology companies continue to pursue business opportunities and industrial partnerships in the Chinese market. China's advantages extend far beyond the size of its market, said Meng Pu, chairman of Qualcomm China, at an AI industry conference in Shenyang, Northeast China's Liaoning Province, on Saturday, according to People's Daily-affiliated Jintai Information. China's comprehensive industrial system, diverse application scenarios, vibrant innovation ecosystem and large pool of skilled engineers provide favorable conditions for new technologies to progress from technical validation and product development to large-scale application, Meng said. China is not only an important market but also a major global force in accelerating the deployment and large-scale application of new technologies, Meng said, pointing to the country's growing importance as AI expands across industries. Qualcomm has worked with Chinese companies for more than three decades, through the evolution of 3G, 4G and 5G mobile communications and the mobile internet. Last year, it teamed up with Chinese mobile operators, device manufacturers and AI model developers to launch an AI acceleration initiative. The automotive sector in China illustrates how such partnerships translate into commercial applications. Since 2021, Qualcomm's Snapdragon Digital Chassis solutions have supported Chinese automakers in more than 300 connected vehicle models, according to Meng. Qualcomm is not alone in highlighting opportunities in China. During a meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao on Thursday, Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook voiced optimism about China's development prospects and vowed to further expand the company's business in the country. The two sides also discussed AI development and bilateral economic ties, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM). US chipmaker Intel also announced a strategic collaboration with China's Lens Technology in July, aimed at developing new technologies for advanced semiconductor packaging. According to Intel's official statement, the two companies will leverage their respective strengths in advanced semiconductor packaging, precision manufacturing, glass substrate research and development, and process innovation to support the growing demands of AI, data center and specialized computing applications. The continued engagement of US technology companies reflects a broader shift in China's role in global innovation, veteran tech industry analyst Liu Dingding told the Global Times on Sunday. Once viewed primarily as a vast consumer market and destination for large-scale technology deployment, China is increasingly emerging as a hub for developing, testing and commercializing advanced technologies, Liu said. "For multinational companies, deeper integration into China's innovation ecosystem can accelerate commercialization, while Chinese manufacturers can leverage international partnerships to advance industrial upgrading," Liu said. "Such complementary strengths offer opportunities for both sides to benefit from AI's expansion into more industries." The corporate emphasis on cooperation comes as China and the US seek to strengthen communication on AI. During their eighth round of economic and trade consultations in September, the two sides established an AI dialogue and held their first discussions on AI-related risks and benefits. Another dialogue is scheduled before the end of November, according to MOFCOM. During Thursday's meeting with Cook, Wang said China advocates safe, controllable and inclusive AI development and cooperation on AI governance. He also expressed hope that Apple would help promote stable China-US economic and trade relations. Liu, the expert, said the continued engagement between US technology companies and their Chinese partners highlights the commercial logic of cooperation despite bilateral technological differences. "Decoupling and disrupting supply chains is neither realistic nor in the interests of businesses," he said, adding that multinational technology companies can also serve as bridges for communication between the two countries' technology industries.

item.title: 17th Media Forum China-Germany held in Heidelberg, stressing media role in strengthening China-Germany relations
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 18:15:00
The 17th Media Forum China-Germany hosted by the Global Times is held in Heidelberg, Germany, from October 14 to 16, 2026. The 17th Media Forum China-Germany, hosted by the Global Times, was held in Heidelberg, Germany, from October 14 to 16. The forum serves as an important platform for strengthening media ties, fostering mutual understanding and exploring how the press can contribute to the healthy and stable development of China-Germany relations. Senior journalists, leaders of major media organizations, and experts and scholars from China and Germany, gathered on the banks of the Neckar River for in-depth discussions on 10 topics, including China-Germany relations, global security, artificial intelligence governance, economic and trade cooperation, green development, global governance and media responsibility. They actively explored shared interests between China and Germany in areas such as trade and investment, technological development, green development and media cooperation, seeking new approaches to deepening mutual understanding and cooperation amid a complex international landscape. Changes in the global landscape unseen in a century are accelerating now, while challenges such as geopolitical conflicts and trade protectionism are becoming increasingly intertwined. As two of the world's major economies, China and Germany maintain close ties in trade and investment, science and technology, and the green transition. Their bilateral relationship is important not only to the development of the two countries, but also to China-Europe cooperation and global economic stability. Against the backdrop of a complex and changing international situation and persistent differences in perceptions, strengthening direct dialogue and fostering mutual understanding and trust have become particularly important. In February, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited China with a business delegation. The leaders of the two countries exchanged views on China-Germany relations, international and regional issues, and economic policies. Both sides agreed to promote the continuous new development of the all-round strategic partnership, promote dialogue and cooperation and uphold multilateralism and free trade. The bilateral relationship not only bears on the interests of both countries, but also has significant impact on Europe and the world. Subsequently, several German ministers visited China in succession, sustaining the momentum of high-level exchanges and advancing deeper cooperation. At the second meeting of the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultation Mechanism, held from October 8 to 9 in Beijing, China and the EU reached a 16-point consensus covering trade and investment, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform during high-level talks in Beijing on Thursday and Friday, marking concrete progress in efforts to manage bilateral economic differences. Against this backdrop, the 17th Media Forum China-Germany aims to further strengthen the role of the media in both countries as a bridge for communication. Through face-to-face exchanges, it seeks to enhance mutual understanding and trust, objectively present areas of consensus and differences between the two sides on major international issues, and expand opportunities for cooperation between Chinese and German media through mutual respect and candid dialogue. It also provides a platform for bringing the peoples of the two countries closer together and bridging gaps in mutual perceptions. In his opening remarks, Bai Long, deputy editor-in-chief of the Global Times, said that the Media Forum China-Germany has been held for 17 sessions and that cooperation between China and Germany has long been characterized by deeply interconnected interests, with each side having a stake in the other. In his view, the pens and cameras in the hands of media professionals can create divergent perceptions, but they can also build bridges of understanding. Bai called for diverse perspectives to be tested and refined through debate to produce sound insights, strengthen mutual trust between China and Germany and between China and Europe, and contribute the media community's voice of reason to the world. During the forum, discussions among Chinese and German participants addressed differences in their understanding of the international situation and industrial policies, while also examining their shared practical interests in technological innovation, the green transition and multilateral cooperation. From debates over the broader international order to specific industrial partnerships and journalistic practices, the exchanges helped clarify each side's concerns and gave more concrete meaning to the shared goal of cooperation. Since its launch in 2010, the Media Forum China-Germany has been held for 17 consecutive sessions and has gradually become an important platform for high-level dialogue and mutual understanding among major media organizations in the two countries. In the face of profound changes in the international landscape, the roundtable will continue to serve as a bridge for communication, promote deeper exchanges and cooperation between Chinese and German media, and inject more constructive momentum into the sound and stable development of bilateral relations. Meanwhile, the Global Times "Overseas China Week" photo exhibition also came to Heidelberg. During the media forum, the photo exhibition titled "Green and Innovation: China and Germany Embarking on Vibrant Future" was successfully held. The "Overseas China Week" is an international cultural communication and dialogue initiative launched by the Global Times to promote cross-cultural exchanges, mutual learning among civilizations, and media cooperation with other countries. The initiative has previously held themed exhibitions and promotional activities in Kazakhstan, Argentina, Brazil, South Korea, South Africa and Kyrgyzstan, receiving positive responses.

item.title: Nearly 20% rise in Taiwan residents' trips to mainland in first 8 months shows cross-Straits exchanges are an 'irresistible trend'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 18:04:00
Participants in a cross-Strait journalism camp pose for a photo at the Mutianyu section of the Great Wall in Beijing, capital of China. Photo: Xinhua Despite an orange travel warning remaining in place for the Chinese mainland, the latest statistics from Taiwan's regional tourism authorities show that residents of the island made a total of 2.492 million visits to the mainland in the first eight months of this year, a year-on-year increase of 19.63 percent. The mainland remained Taiwan residents' second-most popular outbound travel destination in the eight months, according to the department's latest figures, the Xinhua News Agency reported late Saturday. Monthly trips to the mainland exceeded 300,000 from March through August, with double-digit year-on-year growth recorded in each month, Xinhua said. Cross-Straits people-to-people exchanges continue to deepen, driven by shared cultural roots and ethnic heritage, despite attempts by the DPP authorities to obstruct cross-Straits travel and instill fear among Taiwan residents, a mainland expert said, describing closer exchanges as an irresistible trend. The total number of outbound trips by Taiwan residents rose 15.24 percent year-on-year over the same period, while trips to the mainland grew at a faster rate, underscoring strong demand for mainland travel, according to Xinhua. "Grandpas and grandmas like joining group tours to Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and Southwest China's Yunnan Province, while young people follow Xiaohongshu to 'check in' at places like Chongqing and Shanghai on independent trips," a student from the Taiwan region told Xinhua. The student added that trips to the mainland have become increasingly common among people around them, and everyone is happy to post nice photos and share their experiences on social media. Cross-Straits exchanges continue to grow because people on both sides share the same cultural roots and ethnic heritage, said Zhang Wensheng, deputy dean and a professor at the Taiwan Research Institute at Xiamen University, adding that their sense of connection is growing stronger as exchanges become increasingly close. "This trend reflects the fact that people-to-people exchanges across the Taiwan Straits are an irresistible trend," Zhang added. Meanwhile, the mainland has introduced policies offering incentives to attract Taiwan residents, especially young people. With continued economic development and an improving environment, the mainland offers more opportunities for tourism, education, and employment, the expert said. "As a result, many Taiwan residents are still willing to visit the mainland despite obstacles imposed by the DPP authorities." However, Taiwan has maintained the orange warning for the mainland, Hong Kong and Macao since June 27, 2024. Orange is the second-highest warning level in Taiwan's four-tier travel advisory system. An orange warning advises the public to avoid nonessential travel to the affected destinations, according to local media reports. The Taiwan authorities, driven by their political ideology of "Taiwan independence," have sought to hinder people-to-people exchanges across the Straits and restrict travel to the mainland, including issuing the so-called orange travel alert and using political rhetoric to instill fear among Taiwan residents. However, these measures have not achieved their intended effect, Zhang said. "The reality is clear: Do Taiwan residents face danger or threats when visiting the mainland? By seeing the mainland for themselves, they can form their own judgments and assess the claims made by the DPP authorities. For most Taiwan residents, a visit to the mainland is an opportunity to see the facts firsthand and distinguish fact from fiction," he noted. For some time, the DPP authorities have put their own political interests above people's well-being, Chen Binhua, a spokesperson for the Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, said on October 14. Completely ignoring the calls and demands of Taiwan's tourism industry and the general public, they have deliberately erected barriers and obstructed cross-Straits tourism exchanges, hampering the recovery of Taiwan's tourism industry and causing serious losses to businesses and residents, Chen said. The DPP authorities should change course, heed public opinion, remove restrictions and obstacles to cross-Straits people-to-people exchanges and tourism cooperation, and resume mainland residents' travel to Taiwan as soon as possible. Otherwise, they will face growing opposition and rejection from people in Taiwan, the spokesperson warned.

item.title: Canton Fair helps companies expand in BRI markets through partnerships, tailored solutions
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 17:55:00
Buyers and exhibitors gather at the 140th Canton Fair in Guangzhou, South China's Guangdong Province, on October 16, 2026. Photo: VCG At Wandisplay Technology's booth, an Indonesian buyer spent several minutes testing the company's app and checking the accuracy of a new smart wristband before placing an order for 2,000 units on the spot. Such scenes are unfolding across the exhibition halls of the 140th China Import and Export Fair, commonly known as the Canton Fair, where buyers from around the world began exploring products and negotiating orders on Thursday. BRI markets move to the fore Liu Yupei, sales director at Wandisplay Technology, told the Global Times on Thursday that this was the company's second time participating in the Canton Fair, but its business in previously smaller markets across the Middle East, Africa and South America had grown noticeably, particularly in countries and regions covered by Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) cooperation. "More than 400,000 units in new orders came through the last edition of the fair in April," Liu said. Guangzhou Chengzhi Intelligent Machinery Technology Co (CZI), a drone-payload maker, received more than 200 orders worth nearly 10 million yuan ($1.5 million) at its first Canton Fair in April, mostly from Southeast Asia and Eastern Europe. Zhang Kai, deputy president of CZI, told the Global Times that BRI partner countries and regions had seen rapid growth over the past six months and would be the company's priority markets in the near future. Chongqing Huifan Technology is showcasing a palm-vein authentication terminal that works without physical contact, designed for retail stores and smart campuses. Sales manager Zhou Nana told the Global Times that overseas revenue rose about 25 percent in the first half of 2026, with BRI markets such as Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan now a priority. "We hope that through the Canton Fair, we can introduce more new products to markets in countries [and regions] participating in the BRI. On the first day, purchasing agents from countries such as Cameroon came to discuss potential orders," Zhou said. At CVTE's booth, a Brazilian buyer watched a staff member turn a hand-drawn cube into a rotatable 3D model on an interactive display and immediately began discussing a potential purchase. "This is exactly what we need," said Max Goldberg, who had come specifically to find AI-powered education products suited to Brazilian classrooms. Guangzhou-based CVTE, a leading global provider of consumer and commercial LCD display technology, has established local operations and service networks in 33 countries and regions and services more than 140 markets, according to Duan Yu, the company's chief strategic resources officer. These small encounters reflect a broader shift during the first phase of the 140th Canton Fair, which runs through Monday. Buyers from BRI partner countries and regions are arriving not with generic orders but with specific demands. The companies closing deals are those willing to redesign products, rework service models and maintain a presence in the market long after their shipments arrive. Localization and after-sales power Customized products are only half of the story. Local operations and after-sales service help companies build lasting relationships with customers. Must Energy (Guangdong) Tech Co., Ltd. has established offices, delivery hubs and service teams across BRI markets, from Central Asia to Africa and Latin America. It operates more than 20 service centers worldwide and provides household energy solutions tailored to these markets. "Buyers visit our booth at the Canton Fair by day and come to visit our factory in Foshan [in South China's Guangdong Province] by night," Wu Changhua, chairman and president of MUST Energy, told the Global Times on Friday. Wu said the company plans to establish business and sales service centers, open warehouses and expand local services in more BRI markets. Foshan is about an hour's drive from Guangzhou, the host city of the Canton Fair. At the factory of Namkoo New Energy Technology Co. in Foshan, the Global Times met Eric Ong Lim, president of Mindanao Rock and a Canton Fair buyer from the Philippines. Lim visited the factory on Friday to inspect the production line and discuss closer cooperation. "Namkoo is very famous in the Philippines. We have already been talking there. They have an office, so they have many customers," Lim told the Global Times. After the visit his assessment was clear: "I'm very satisfied with the product quality and much more confident to invest than before." A two-way trade bridge While Chinese companies are finding BRI customers and partners at the Canton Fair, businesses from BRI markets are also using the platform to reach buyers worldwide. The Canton Fair's import section serves as a bridge for two-way trade. At this edition, it will run during the second phase, from October 23 to 27, and the third phase, from October 31 to November 4. In recent editions, the proportion of exhibitors from BRI countries in the import section has continued to rise, the Global Times learned from the organizer. The Canton Fair's global partnership network now spans 112 countries and regions and includes 238 overseas institutions, industry associations and major purchasing companies. Since the import section was created in 2007, more than 15,000 overseas companies from over 100 countries and regions have taken part. For many of those exhibitors, the fair is not only a door into China but a bridge to buyers from other countries. The broader trade figures provide context for these business exchanges. In the first three quarters of 2026, China's trade with BRI partner countries reached 20.37 trillion yuan, up 17.1 percent year-on-year, with imports rising 17.9 percent, slightly faster than exports at 16.6 percent, according to statistics from the General Administration of Customs. What is changing at the Canton Fair is not simply who is buying, but what a deal includes. A wristband order comes after a buyer tests the data. A conversation at a booth turns into a service network that remains in place long after the shipment arrives. For BRI partner countries, these partnerships offer access to products, technical support and local services. For Chinese companies, they create opportunities to build lasting customer relationships and expand their market presence.

item.title: Researchers identify world's 1st known juvenile fossil of Huphsuchus dating back around 247 mln years in C. China's Hubei
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 16:22:00
Reconstruction of a juvenile Huphsuchus in its natural habitat Photo: Courtesy of Hubei Institute of Geosciences An international collaborative study has recently confirmed the world’s first juvenile fossil of Huphsuchus, an extinct genus of small marine reptiles dating back approximately 247 million years, discovered in Yuan’an county, Central China’s Hubei Province, the Global Times learned from the Hubei Institute of Geosciences, Hubei Geological Bureau, on Sunday. The research has been published in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society. Wang Yinuo of Peking University, and Zou Yarui, a senior engineer from the Hubei Institute of Geosciences, Hubei Geological Bureau, are the paper’s co-first authors. Researched and named in 1972 by Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian, Huphsuchus was a prehistoric marine reptile that lived in shallow marine waters during the Early Triassic, approximately 247 million years ago. The genus represents one of the early evolutionary branches of reptiles that diversified into marine environments following the end-Permian mass extinction. More than 50 years of research has found Huphsuchus fossils only near the border of Yuan’an and Nanzhang counties in Hubei. However, as nearly all known specimens are adults, some researchers have suggested that its juveniles may be the same species as Nanchangosaurus, fossils of which were discovered in the same geological strata in the area and first reported in 1959. In 2023, the Hubei Institute of Geosciences began ecological restoration and emergency fossil excavations at Yinggou Quarry, a major marine reptile fossil site in Yuan’an county. During quarry slope clearance, researchers discovered a partially preserved fossil skeleton, designated YGM17-1, in the fossil-bearing layer numbered 17. After careful restoration and examination, researchers confirmed that the specimen belonged to a juvenile Huphsuchus, rather than Nanchangosaurus or other marine reptiles. According to Zou, the research team conducted detailed morphological and comparative anatomical studies of the specimen, confirming that it was distinct from Nanchangosaurus and exhibited the characteristic features of Huphsuchus, including 10 cervical vertebrae and 26 to 28 dorsal vertebrae. The fossil specimen also exhibits key characteristics of juvenile ichthyosaur reptiles, including short forelimbs, incomplete ossification of the humerus and ribs, and unossified wrist bones. After comparing 20 previously reported fossils and conducting morphological and statistical analyses, the researchers found that despite similarities in skull features and vertebral counts, Huphsuchus and Nanchangosaurus differ significantly in several key traits. According to Li Jiangli, head of the joint research team and director of the paleontology center at the Hubei Institute of Geosciences, Yuan’an county hosts a globally rare assemblage of Early Triassic marine reptile fossils, with abundant, exceptionally well-preserved Huphsuchus specimens of significant scientific value. The Yuan’an fauna, together with four other fossil assemblages spanning the Early to Late Triassic, forms a rare, nearly complete evolutionary sequence of Triassic marine reptiles in South China, offering valuable insights into their origins, diversification, evolution and extinction while presenting new scientific challenges, Li said. At present, the joint research team is stepping up the restoration and study of Yuan’an’s prehistoric marine reptile fossils, seeking new insights into their evolution, physiology, behavior and environments in which they lived, Li added.

item.title: Beijing tackles rapid aging as capital expected to become super-aged society by 2035
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 16:08:00
Elderly people relax and chat at Ritan Park in Beijing on October 9, 2026. Photo: IC Beijing is expected to become a super-aged society by 2035, with one-third of its population aged 60 or older. To address this trend, the Chinese capital has stepped up efforts in recent years to strengthen legal protections for elderly care, improve social security, promote the integration of elderly care services with related industries, expand medical-care partnerships and reinforce its multi-tiered pension system, Beijing Daily reported on Saturday. According to data released at a recent industry forum ahead of the Double Ninth Festival, also known as the Chongyang Festival, in Beijing, Beijing had 5.288 million permanent residents aged 60 and above at the end of 2025, accounting for 24.3 percent of its population. The proportion is expected to exceed 33 percent by 2035, meaning one in every three residents will be aged 60 or above, according to Beijing Daily. As a megacity, Beijing is stepping up efforts to address its rapidly aging population. In January, it introduced its first comprehensive, foundational local regulation on elderly care services, making it the first city in China to establish a three-tier elderly care service network covering districts, subdistricts (townships) and communities (villages) through local legislation. Beijing has also raised basic pensions for urban and rural residents year after year and established a system of allowances and subsidies for elderly care services. In 2025, it disbursed about 3.51 billion yuan ($525 million) in such allowances and subsidies, benefiting older people facing financial hardship, those unable to care for themselves and those of advanced age, with a total of 11.958 million beneficiary instances. Meanwhile, Beijing is pursuing an integrated approach to developing elderly care services and related industries. To date, Beijing has 620 registered elderly care institutions, 168 regional care centers and more than 1,500 community care stations, providing a total of 155,000 beds across various types of facilities. In response to the trend toward an increasingly aged population, Beijing prioritizes care for the oldest-old population through preferential services, fee reductions and waivers, regular welfare visits and emergency assistance. Given that the vast majority of older people prefer to age at home, Beijing is continuing to develop a 15-minute elderly care service network. Beijing has nearly 3,000 registered meal service sites serving older residents, covering 90 percent of the city's urban and rural communities. Over the next three years, the city plans to add 30,000 home-based elderly care beds. Official statistics showed that China had 323.38 million people aged 60 and above at the end of 2025, accounting for 23 percent of its population. Rising care needs among older people with disabilities, dementia and those living alone are intensifying demand for care services, while a shortage of professional elderly care workers remains a key challenge, according to the Legal Daily. item.title: Croatian PM meets Chinese FM, voices willingness to expand bilateral cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 09:47:00
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic meets with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, in Zagreb, Croatia, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang) Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic met with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi here on Saturday, expressing Croatia's willingness to further expand cooperation with China. During the meeting, Plenkovic asked Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, to convey his sincere greetings to the Chinese leadership, saying that he looks forward to visiting China at an early date and meeting with the leadership. Relations between Croatia and China have continued to improve, underpinned by mutual respect and sincere cooperation, Plenkovic said. Chinese enterprises have participated in infrastructure projects in Croatia, including roads, bridges and tunnels, he said, noting that the Peljesac Bridge has played a significant role in improving connectivity between different parts of the country. The Croatian side highly appreciates these contributions and welcomes continued participation of Chinese enterprises in the country's development, he said. Croatia is willing to further expand cooperation with China in such areas as tourism, photovoltaics and wind power, he added. The prime minister also welcomes the launch of direct flights between Croatia and China, looking forward to closer exchanges between their peoples. Stressing that Croatia attaches great importance to cooperation with China under the China-Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs) framework and the Belt and Road Initiative, Plenkovic said Croatia is willing to continue contributing to these efforts and looks forward to the early resumption of CEEC-China leaders' meeting mechanism to create new opportunities for closer high-level exchanges between the two sides. For his part, Wang conveyed the Chinese leadership's good wishes to Plenkovic and welcomed him to visit China at a mutually convenient time. Wang said China was among the first major countries to establish diplomatic relations with Croatia, adding that bilateral relations have enjoyed healthy, steady and sustainable development under the strategic guidance of the two countries' leaders. China and Croatia treat each other with sincerity and mutual respect and have established a mature, long-term comprehensive cooperative partnership, Wang said, noting that this has been the right choice made by both sides. China is willing to further elevate bilateral relations on this foundation, he added. Moreover, Wang said China cherishes its traditional friendship with Croatia and is willing to translate it into a strong driving force for bilateral relations in the new era. Wang also said China respects the choices of the Croatian people and Croatia's governance model, and is willing to deepen mutually beneficial cooperation to support each other's development and revitalization. China values people-to-people and cultural exchanges with Croatia and has introduced measures, including unilateral visa-free access and direct flights, to facilitate travel and enhance mutual understanding between the two peoples, Wang stressed. In addition, Wang noted that China firmly believes that China and the European Union (EU) are partners, not rivals. China supports European integration and Croatia's efforts to achieve faster development through this process, and hopes Croatia will play a constructive role in deepening China-EU cooperation, Wang added. Meanwhile, Wang stressed that China and CEECs share a practical need to strengthen exchanges and cooperation. Such cooperation is entirely open and transparent and contributes to European integration, he said. China is willing to strengthen cooperation with interested countries in the region through established mechanisms, Wang said, noting that China appreciates Croatia's positive attitude in this regard and is ready to use the 15th anniversary of the China-CEEC cooperation mechanism next year as an opportunity to reinvigorate mutually beneficial cooperation between the two sides. The two sides also exchanged views on China-EU economic and trade relations. Plenkovic said that EU countries, including Croatia, have concerns about trade imbalances. Participants at the recent EU summit spoke positively of the consensus reached through the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism and expressed hope that the two sides would continue to strengthen communication and dialogue to properly address their differences, he said. Wang said that trade issues between China and the EU stem from the international division of labor and market demand. Imports of high-quality, competitively priced Chinese goods benefit European consumers and help curb inflation, reflecting demand in the European market, and there is no so-called "overcapacity" problem, he noted. China is willing to import more high-value-added products from Europe and hopes the EU will ease restrictions on exports to China, Wang said. China is committed to promoting balanced growth in bilateral trade, with both sides moving forward rather than backward and expanding shared benefits rather than diminishing them, he added. He also said China is ready to strengthen dialogue with the EU on the basis of equality and mutual benefit, jointly uphold free trade and advance open and inclusive economic globalization. Meanwhile, Plenkovic briefed Wang on the situation in the Western Balkans. Wang said that China does not interfere in the internal affairs of countries in the region and hopes that all countries will enhance understanding, rebuild mutual trust and coexist in harmony through dialogue. China is willing to play a constructive role in line with the needs of countries in the region, he added. Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic meets with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, in Zagreb, Croatia, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang)

item.title: Paraguay tech minister's response to China's countermeasures a deliberate attempt to shift responsibility
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17 16:28:00
Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT Days after China announced countermeasures against Paraguay's Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Emigdio Villate Samaniego over his wrong moves on the Taiwan question, he wrote lengthy posts on social media, which Chinese experts describe as an attempt to shift responsibility by framing the move over his own misconduct as targeting the entire country. In a post on his X account, Villate called the countermeasures “a certification that what we have been doing since 2023 is the correct path.” He also declared that Paraguay's relationship with the Taiwan region would "never be on the table as a bargaining chip." His remarks may sound defiant, but they turn cause and effect on their head: They recast interference in China's internal affairs as "sovereign diplomacy," and portray collusion with separatist forces as "cooperation between two democracies." Here is why China took the countermeasures against Villate and Belize Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Francis Fonseca. In announcing the measures, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry pointed out that certain politicians in Paraguay and Belize willingly serve as chess pieces for Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities in their pursuit of independence by soliciting external support. "Their visits to Taiwan and reception of 'Taiwan independence' separatist forces in their countries constitute severe interference in China's internal affairs. They also attacked and smeared China by spreading the 'Chinese cyberattack' disinformation, causing egregious impact in the world," the spokesperson said. Apparently, the word that apparently struck a nerve with Villate was chess piece, or "pawn" as he puts it in his social media post. Villate’s decision to speak out loudly several days after the countermeasures were announced was an attempt to salvage his credibility after being exposed for his collusion with “Taiwan independence” separatist forces, Xin Qiang, director of the Taiwan Studies Center at Fudan University, told the Global Times on Monday, adding that Villate is putting on a stunt for people in Paraguay and DPP authorities to gain support. Villate seeks to turn China’s countermeasures against him into a political narrative about Paraguay "defending its right." Yet his refusal to reflect on his erroneous actions, and his determination to "accelerate" them, only further reinforce the impression that he is acting as a “pawn.” Villate also sought to frame his attempt to pursue certain so-called technology cooperation projects with DPP authorities as being in the interest of Paraguay, despite what experts describe as limited benefits and enormous costs in various fields. “Villate wants to convince people that his actions will bring prosperity to Paraguay, but there is no such thing as a free lunch,” Zhang Wensheng, deputy dean and a professor at the Taiwan Research Institute at Xiamen University, told the Global Times, adding that the move actually puts Paraguay's national interests and its people's welfare at risk. For years, voices within Paraguay's agricultural sector have called for reconsidering the country's diplomatic policy, hoping to gain access to China's market for beef, soybeans and other products. For a developing country seeking to expand agricultural exports, attract investment and upgrade its industries, the absence of normal diplomatic relations with one of the world's largest economies creates tangible obstacles. There is one thing Villate gets right: Beijing's message "deserves careful reading." Unfortunately, he has read it entirely backward. Being the only country in South America that still maintains so-called diplomatic relations with the Taiwan authorities is hardly a badge to boast about. Rather, it highlights how far Paraguay has moved against the prevailing international trend. More troublingly, the erroneous actions of certain politicians like Villate will also be borne by the country and its people. Ordinary people across the world want to pursue better lives through good jobs and development rather than by interfering in other countries’ internal affairs. Binding one's future to "Taiwan independence" separatist forces is not a path toward greater autonomy. It is a dead end that risks forfeiting development opportunities and leaving a country increasingly isolated internationally. The author is a reporter with the Global Times. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

item.title: No bullying the small, no blackmail by the small: China's South China Sea rule
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 18:11:00
Philippines South China Sea Illustration: Liu Xidan/Global Times Recent remarks by Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan have been portrayed in Manila as a threat. In fact, they restate a consistent Chinese position: firm defense of territorial sovereignty and maritime rights, together with a preference for peace, restraint and managing differences through direct dialogue. In the South China Sea, China will not use its size to bully the small, nor allow the Philippines to use its smallness to blackmail the strong. China’s approach to territorial and maritime disputes has remained stable for decades. It safeguards its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights while consistently advocating peaceful settlement through bilateral negotiation and consultation. This principle applies not only to the South China Sea but also to other territorial and maritime questions involving its neighbors. The disputes between China and the Philippines have a long history. China maintains that they stem primarily from the Philippines’ occupation of eight features in China’s Nansha Islands beginning in the 1970s and its subsequent claim over Huangyan Island. Overlapping maritime claims also emerged as the international law of the sea developed. Successive Philippine administrations have repeatedly taken actions that have aggravated tensions, including arrests of fishermen from the Chinese mainland and Taiwan, and the unilateral initiation of the South China Sea arbitration case, which China opposed as contrary to prior bilateral understandings and the principle of state consent. China regards its responses to infringement and provocation as legitimate measures to defend its rights. The equality of states under the United Nations Charter and general international law does not give any country a free hand to manufacture incidents at sea. Where a state has illegally occupied another state’s territory, the latter retains, in principle, the right of self-defense. China has exercised considerable restraint, prioritizing regional stability and preserving space for dialogue. That restraint should not be mistaken for the absence of limits. The disparity in national strength, particularly maritime capabilities, between China and the Philippines is an objective fact. Manila cannot expect its repeated provocations, public smearing, and the suspension of military communication channels to be met indefinitely with silence. China has treated the Philippines as an equal neighbor, but restraint is not unlimited. Effective management of maritime differences depends substantially on whether the Philippine government can restrain its military and coast guard. Persistent difficulties in bilateral relations serve neither country’s interests and are particularly damaging to the Philippines’ development. Regional countries should jointly safeguard the region’s hard-won peace and development. Whenever the two sides have moved toward dialogue, certain forces within the Philippines, particularly its military and coast guard, have manufactured incidents to disrupt progress. These forces appear driven less by public welfare than by external powers’ preferences and their own political or institutional interests. If Manila calls for dialogue while allowing these forces to create friction and stoke anti-China sentiment, bilateral communication mechanisms will struggle to function. China and the Philippines are permanent neighbors. Maritime disputes do not change this geographic reality. External military equipment and joint military exercises cannot reverse the regional balance of power. Nor can repeated invocations of a “China threat” narrative resolve the Philippines’ domestic development challenges. Manila may believe that militarization and maritime incidents demonstrate its value as a “frontline platform” for the US and other Western countries, securing stronger security guarantees and economic benefits. Such expectations overlook external powers’ independent strategic calculations. External powers may provide equipment and diplomatic backing while using the Philippines’ geographic location to strengthen their military posture. Their support does not guarantee a willingness to bear the costs of escalation. If a crisis spirals out of control, distant powers can reduce their involvement, leaving the Philippines to face the consequences. History offers repeated warnings about tying national security to another country’s strategic agenda. Manila should weigh that risk carefully. China-Philippines relations stand at a crossroads. Continued tolerance of maritime provocations will invite bolder moves and further damage bilateral ties. The immediate priority for the Marcos government should be to restrain adventurist impulses within its military and coast guard, halt provocations and information operations directed against China, and return to bilateral dialogue and consultation. Only sustained dialogue, supported by restraint and consistent action, can manage differences and stabilize ties. The author is director of the Research Center for International and Regional Studies at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

item.title: 'Forced labor' in Xinjiang's salmon industry, too? The New York Times has lost it: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 23:44:00
A salmon farm in Nilka County, Ili Kazak Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Photo: VCG In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. Recently, The New York Times published a purported in-depth investigative report about the fish farming industry. The article adopts the posture of a "neutral" investigation, citing global research and evidence from multiple sources. It ranges from Peruvian fishing vessels and fishmeal processing plants to offshore aquaculture pens in Norway. Yet in the second half of the article, the focus takes a sharp turn toward the salmon industry in Northwest China's Xinjiang, devoting extensive coverage to recycling familiar allegations such as "forced labor." Read closely, the report reveals a familiar pattern: In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. The report offers no evidence from firsthand interviews to support its claims about Xinjiang. Instead, it pieced together much of its narrative from vague attributions with phrases such as "claim," "accuse," and "most likely." By using documented problems in the seafood industry in other parts of the world to shape readers' perceptions in the first half, the article encourages them to assume that the claims made in the second half are equally well substantiated. However, the report provides no solid evidence that similar problems exist in Xinjiang, while packaging subjective speculation as so-called "investigative findings." Such journalistic practices run directly counter to the most basic standards of media credibility. Why are US media outlets willing to lose their credibility just to push out similar fake reports? The real aim, it would appear, is to lend support to Washington's unilateral sanctions targeting Xinjiang. From cotton and tomatoes to sunflower seeds and dumplings, and from solar photovoltaics to polysilicon, the pattern remains the same, with the focus now shifting to Xinjiang's cold-water fish industry: Any competitive industry that benefits Xinjiang's local communities is targeted with the "human rights" cudgel, as negative media coverage is paired with unilateral sanctions to suppress Chinese competitive industries and contain development in China's western regions. It's important to point out that what these sanctions are really aimed at is the employment and development rights of people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang. In fact, Xinjiang's salmon industry is a prime example of how local resources can be harnessed to turn geographical disadvantages into drivers of development. It is also a tangible achievement of China's campaign to develop its western regions in the new era. Nilka County in the Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture benefits from glacial meltwater flowing down from the Tianshan Mountains. The water remains cold and rich in dissolved oxygen throughout the year, and its excellent quality provides exceptional natural conditions for cold-water fish farming. Technologies such as automated feeding, underwater cleaning robots, and semi-closed recirculating aquaculture systems help minimize pollution, while uneaten feed and fish waste can be processed into organic fertilizer. The farming process emphasizes raising fish without medication and at low stocking densities. Companies in the industry have also obtained multiple international food safety certifications. Their products serve the domestic market and are exported to countries across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. They have even gained access to Singapore, a market known for its stringent food standards. Turning desert landscapes into productive fisheries and snow-capped mountains into a source of premium seafood is an industrial success achieved through Chinese ingenuity and hard work. The benefits to people's livelihoods, brought about by industrial development, are being tangibly enjoyed by the people of all ethnic groups. Under a model that combines leading enterprises, employment in industrial parks and social security, some farming and herding families whose livelihoods have revolved around pastoralism for generations have moved into companies and become industrial workers, earning stable wages. Some herders also receive dividends through equity investments. Many young people have chosen to return to their hometowns for work closer to home. The salmon industry has also spurred the growth of fish-themed agritourism, specialty restaurants, rural tourism, and related businesses, opening up additional sources of income and giving fresh impetus to rural vitalization. These concrete, visible improvements in people's lives stand in stark contrast to the falsehoods propagated by some Western media outlets. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. It is hoped that some Western media outlets that pride themselves on being "fair and objective" will drop their self-deceptive tactics and go to Xinjiang to see the real production scenes for themselves, listen to workers on the ground describe their own experiences, and gain a firsthand understanding of what human rights really mean to the people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang - and what rights they genuinely enjoy and deserve to have respected.
